blocks.text: **Organizational-dynamics bridge:** Diane Vaughan's "normalization of deviance" — the process by which warnings are incrementally rationalized as acceptable until catastrophic failure — was developed from the Challenger disaster but applies directly to corporate crime. The organizational mechanism is identical to technical debt accumulation: each small violation that goes unpunished resets the threshold of what counts as normal; compliance costs are deferred; warnings are reframed as acceptable risk; eventually the system fails catastrophically (Enron, Boeing 737 MAX, Volkswagen emissions). In engineering orgs, the structural conditions that produce this — performance pressure from above, diffuse responsibility ("someone else will catch it"), and the absence of independent auditors with real power — are the same conditions Vaughan identifies in corporate crime. The Fraud Triangle (pressure + opportunity + rationalization) maps precisely to: unreachable quarterly targets (pressure), access to complex financial instruments without effective controls (opportunity), and "everyone does it" / "the lawyers signed off" (rationalization).
